vLLM reduces KV‑cache waste by treating the cache as a set of logical blocks that are mapped to physical memory pages, a design called PagedAttention that mirrors operating‑system paging [P0e0bee546fc5][P3367ea1ac7de]. When a request generates several output sequences—either through parallel sampling or beam search—the prompt portion of the cache is stored once as physical blocks and referenced by the logical blocks of every new sequence. In parallel sampling the system “forks’’ the original sequence, creating multiple child sequences that all point to the same prompt blocks; each iteration then “appends’’ a new token to each child while the shared prompt cache remains untouched [P34cd29a8ebec][Pbe8811fbeba5]. Because the prompt accounts for roughly 12 % of total KV memory, this sharing yields measurable savings [Pf50ce35e4c88].

When a child sequence eventually needs to write into a block that is still shared, vLLM employs a copy‑on‑write scheme. The block engine tracks a reference count for each physical block; if the count exceeds one, a new physical block is allocated, the contents are copied, and the reference count is decremented [P402025ed7055]. The second sample can then write directly to the now‑exclusive block. This mechanism allows the majority of the prompt cache to stay shared while only the final logical block of each sample is duplicated, dramatically cutting memory use for long inputs [P402025ed7055][Pf50ce35e4c88].

Beam search extends the same principle. All beams start from the same prompt and share its KV cache; as beams diverge, additional blocks are allocated only for the differing suffixes. Empirically, vLLM saves 6–10 % of KV blocks in parallel sampling and up to 55 % in beam search with a width of six, because beams can share larger portions of the cache than independent samples [P6fb6ea0c7fc7][Pf50ce35e4c88]. The centralized KV‑cache manager, shared by all GPU workers, maintains the logical‑to‑physical mapping so that each worker can access the same physical pages without redundant copies [P5c9f646ffa37][P98b2a98bf6c3]. Thus, vLLM’s combination of logical block abstraction, reference‑counted sharing, copy‑on‑write, and the fork/append/free workflow enables efficient KV‑cache sharing across both parallel samples and beam search.

# How does vLLM share KV cache memory across parallel samples and beams?

> **PARTIAL ANSWER — some parts of the question could not be established**
> Evidence-sufficiency score 0.33 (heuristic)
> _Uncalibrated: decided by the heuristic scorer, not a fitted model._

## What the evidence establishes

vLLM reduces KV‑cache memory by letting multiple output sequences reuse the same physical blocks that store the prompt’s key and value states. *[unverified]* The system represents the cache as logical KV blocks that are mapped to physical blocks managed by a single KV‑cache manager shared across all GPU workers [1]. *[partially supported]* When a request is decoded with parallel sampling, vLLM “forks’’ the original prompt sequence into several samples; each forked sequence initially points to the same physical blocks, so the prompt KV cache is shared [2][3]. As generation proceeds, new tokens are appended to each sample. *[unverified]* For tokens that belong to the shared prompt region, the existing physical blocks are read without duplication, while the newly generated KV entries are written into newly allocated physical blocks that are added to the block table [4].

To keep the shared region consistent, vLLM uses a copy‑on‑write scheme. *[unverified]* If a sample needs to modify the last logical block of the shared prompt, the manager checks the reference count of the underlying physical block; when the count exceeds one it allocates a fresh physical block, copies the data, and decrements the count, after which the sample writes its new KV entries to the private block [5]. The other sample can then continue writing directly to the original block because its reference count has dropped to one. *[unverified]* This mechanism enables most of the prompt KV cache to be shared across parallel samples, with only the final logical block being duplicated as needed [5][6].

Beam search follows the same pattern: all beams start from a common prompt and therefore share its KV cache; as beams diverge, each creates its own physical blocks for newly generated tokens, yielding larger overall sharing (up to about 55 % memory saving) compared with independent sampling [7][6]. *[partially supported]*

The evidence does not establish how vLLM guarantees safe concurrent access to the shared KV cache when multiple samples or beams are processed in parallel, nor does it explain how updates are coordinated when beams diverge to keep shared entries consistent. These aspects remain unresolved because the cited sources provide no details on synchronization or consistency mechanisms for concurrent writes.

## What could not be established

- How does vLLM ensure safe concurrent access to the shared KV cache when multiple samples or beams are processed in parallel?
- How does vLLM handle updates to the KV cache when beams diverge during beam search, ensuring that shared entries remain consistent?
